stem: A client with diabetes and loss of protective sensation has a thick plantar callus. The client's usual shoes fit tightly over the callused area. Which teaching by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Avoid cutting or shaving the callus, arrange foot-care evaluation, and use well-fitted footwear that reduces pressure on the callused area.
options.B: Soak the foot before gently shaving the callus, then change footwear only if the callused area becomes painful or starts to redden.
options.C: Apply an over-the-counter medicated callus remover, cover the area afterward, and continue the current shoes while the skin stays intact.
options.D: Pad the callus inside the current shoes and monitor for discomfort before seeking evaluation, because pain should signal when pressure is excessive.

rationale: Loss of protective sensation and plantar callus increase diabetic foot-ulcer risk. The ADA Standards of Care advise avoiding self-care of calluses and recommend well-fitted, pressure-relieving footwear for increased plantar pressures demonstrated by callus; foot-care specialist evaluation and surveillance are appropriate for at-risk feet. NIDDK likewise advises clients with nerve damage to discuss callus care with a foot clinician and not to cut calluses or use medicated callus removers. Therefore A is the best teaching. B and C involve self-treatment that can injure insensate skin. D leaves the pressure source uncorrected and relies on discomfort even though loss of protective sensation can make clinically important injury painless.
educational_objective: Teach clients with diabetic loss of protective sensation and plantar callus to avoid self-cutting or chemical callus removal, obtain appropriate foot-care evaluation, and use well-fitted pressure-relieving footwear rather than waiting for pain to signal tissue injury.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes
source_document_title: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Foot Care, Recommendation 12.31; Foot Care Education for People With Diabetes; Treatment: loss of protective sensation and preulcerative calluses are risk factors; specialized therapeutic footwear is recommended for high-risk clients including those with LOPS or callous formation; initial management includes avoidance of self-care of calluses and well-fitted athletic or walking shoes with customized pressure-relieving orthoses for increased plantar pressures demonstrated by plantar calluses.
source_claim_supported: Diabetic loss of protective sensation and callus increase foot-ulcer risk; self-care of calluses should be avoided and pressure from footwear should be addressed with appropriate well-fitted, pressure-relieving footwear and foot-care support.

supporting_sources.organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
supporting_sources.version_date: Last reviewed January 2017; current NIDDK resource accessed 2026-08-25
supporting_sources.locator: Tips to Take Care of Your Feet > Smooth corns and calluses gently: nerve damage can allow corns/calluses to become ulcers; discuss care with a foot doctor; do not cut corns/calluses or use medicated corn/callus removers because these can damage skin and cause infection. Check your feet every day: foot problems may occur without pain.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Clients with diabetic nerve damage should not cut calluses or use medicated callus removers and should not rely on pain to identify foot injury.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance, printed p. 27: educate clients about prevention and treatment of high-risk health behaviors; educate clients about preventive care and health-maintenance recommendations; assess client ability to manage care in the home environment and plan care accordingly.
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — preventive diabetic foot self-care teaching
correction_summary: Rebuilt the options to eliminate the uniquely-long keyed-answer cue and replace implausible distractors with realistic unsafe self-care choices. The corrected item preserves diabetic foot-risk teaching while making one guideline-supported answer uniquely best and maintaining the Health Promotion and Maintenance blueprint mapping.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Diabetic foot-risk prevention — loss of protective sensation with plantar callus
audit_findings.stem: PASS — clinically coherent risk scenario with LOPS, plantar callus, and a clear pressure source; no hidden assumptions are needed.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects ADA avoidance of callus self-care plus pressure-relieving footwear and appropriate foot-care evaluation; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — home shaving is a plausible self-care misconception but conflicts with guidance to avoid self-care of calluses; waiting for pain is unsafe with LOPS.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — medicated callus removers are specifically discouraged by NIDDK and continuing pressure from tight footwear fails to address a recognized risk factor.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — padding without correcting tight footwear and relying on discomfort are inadequate in a client with impaired protective sensation.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that both avoids injurious self-treatment and addresses ongoing plantar pressure with guideline-supported care.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B and C recommend contraindicated self-treatment; D fails to correct the pressure source and relies on pain despite LOPS.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — the keyed option is not the longest; all options are comparable in length and clinical specificity, with no keyed-only absolute wording.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Health Promotion and Maintenance explicitly includes preventive health teaching, health-maintenance recommendations, and home self-care assessment.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether padding, home callus reduction, or symptom-triggered escalation could be defensible; current ADA and NIDDK guidance excludes self-cutting/chemical removal and supports pressure reduction, while LOPS invalidates pain as a reliable safety trigger. A remains uniquely best.
